$comment: What agentlings may reach outside their sandbox. A connection declares its
own default with 'defaultOn'; the user's departures from those defaults are
recorded in .agentlings/settings.json, never here. Secrets are named, never
written here — put the value in .env under that name and the server passes
it to the connection only. A connection whose secrets are missing is never
live, whatever its default says.
'web' is built in and defaultOn: this is an outreach platform, so reaching
a page is what the crew is for rather than something to be asked for job by
job. Switch it off in Settings. It is our own fetch, which returns readable
text trimmed to maxChars rather than a whole page. Add hosts to 'allow' to
narrow it.
Every connection lists the 'tools' a job may call on it. The list is the
grant: a server offering both reading and acting can be adopted for
reading alone by naming only its reading tools, and anything not named is
refused by the allowlist. It also makes this file say what a connection
can do without anyone having to run it.
'browser' is Playwright MCP (Apache-2.0, Microsoft), fetched by npx so no
code lands in this repo. It is deliberately READ-ONLY: of the 24 tools it
offers, the eight named below read a page and none of them act. Left out
on purpose are click, type, fill_form, press_key, select_option, drag,
drop, file_upload, handle_dialog, evaluate, run_code_unsafe and
network_request — because this app's safety model is a sandbox reviewed
before anything is promoted, and a submitted form cannot be reviewed
afterwards. Adding an acting tool is a decision about that model, not a
line in a list.
It signs in by re-using a session you created yourself: log in once in a
real browser, save the storage state, and point AGENTLINGS_BROWSER_STATE
at the file. The app never sees a password — and with the variable unset
the argument is dropped and browsing works signed out.
External MCP servers take: name, label, description, transport 'stdio',
command, args, tools, and optional secrets {ENV_NAME: 'why it is needed'}.
They ship off by default — they carry credentials and act on the user's
behalf, which is a different decision from reading a page. Keep results
small by design — every token a tool returns is a token the model pays to
read, and for a stdio server that budget is the server's own flags, not
ours: the SDK talks to it directly, so nothing of ours sits in between.

connections.name: web
connections.label: Read web pages
connections.description: Fetches a page and returns its readable text, trimmed. No JavaScript, no sign-ins.

connections.name: browser
connections.label: Use a web browser
connections.description: Opens pages in a real browser and reads what they show, including sites that need JavaScript. Reads only — it cannot click, type or submit anything.
